articles.title: WATCH: Omarion Hampton scores Chargers second TD of game vs Ravens
articles.summary: Los Angeles has their second touchdown of the night after Omarion Hampton found, giving the Chargers a 17-7 lead against the Baltimore Ravens.
articles.body:
Initially, it looked like running back Omarion Hampton would be called short on his fourth-and-goal rushing attempt. However, following a second effort and being pulled into the end zone by offensive lineman Scott Matlock, Hampton got in for the one-yard touchdown to extend the Los Angeles Chargers' lead against the Baltimore Ravens on Monday Night Football.

Here is a look at Hampton's touchdown, courtesy of the NFL's official social media:

This touchdown actually should not have counted, according to ESPN's rules analyst, Russell Yurk. During the broadcast, Yurk explained that Matlock clearly pulling Hampton into the end zone should have been a foul, which would have negated the penalty. If that had been called, Los Angeles may have kicked a field goal instead to make it 13-7.

But since the penalty was not called, the Chargers now have a 17-7 lead shortly before the two-minute warning. Los Angeles will also receive the kickoff to begin the second half.

articles.title: ClutchPoints’ Week 12 2026 College Football Hot Seat Rankings: Is Mike Elko in trouble?
articles.summary: In the 2025 season, 15 coaches were given their walking papers when all was said and done. Some teams hit the jackpot with new hires. Oregon State hired JaMa...
articles.body:
In the 2025 season, 15 coaches were given their walking papers when all was said and done. Some teams hit the jackpot with new hires. Oregon State hired JaMarcus Shephard after letting go of Trent Bray. Oregon State went from a two-win team to contending in the Pac-12. Florida let go of Billy Napier and has improved tremendously with Jon Sumrall as the coach. The big win came at UCLA. The Bruins let go of DeShaun Foster, and new coach Bob Chesney has UCLA as one of the best teams in the nation .

This season, six coaches have already been let go. Maryland moved on from Mike Locksley as the first termination of the year. Dave Doeren from NC State went next, and the Wolfpack has since hired Philip Rivers. Dave Aranda is gone at Baylor, and Phil Longo has been let go by Sam Houston. Mike Norvell was finally fired by Florida State on November 1. Finally, Scotty Walden was fired by UTEP on Monday .

While six coaches are gone already, there will be more who could be joining them in the unemployment line soon.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

There are multiple coaches in their first year with new programs that could be one and done. One of those is Tosh Lupoi at Cal. Cal was a bowl team the last three seasons, but the university decided to move from Justin Wilcox, with the team sitting at 6-5 near the end of the 2025 season. The expectation was for improvement, but the team has bottomed out. After a 3-3 start, Cal has lost four straight and not been competitive. They have lost the games by a combined 167-44. If the horrible form continues the final two games, Lupoi will be rising in the rankings.

Scott Satterfield at Cincinnati could also be in trouble if things continue to trend down. Cincinnati started 4-0, but then lost back-to-back games. The Bearcats then upset Texas Tech, but have since lost three straight. Last week, it was a 41-13 loss to Iowa State. If Cincinnati loses out and misses a bowl for a third time in five years, Satterfield will be in trouble.

Lincoln Riley could also make the list if USC struggles in their final two games. Riley consistently led his teams to the playoffs at Oklahoma, but has yet to do so at USC. At 7-3, USC still has a chance to make a run at the playoffs, but will need help. Still, if they lose out, Riley is likely gone.

Then there are the coaches that should be on the list, but got some recent votes of confidence. Rutgers has been terrible this year, sitting at 2-8 and in last place in the Big Ten. Their lone win in conference play came against Maryland, who promptly fired their coach. Still, the university has declared that Greg Schiano will be back at Rutgers in 2027.

Meanwhile, despite Oklahoma coming into the season with high expectations, Brent Venables has been declared to not be on the hot seat by the Oklahoma Board of Regents. After making the College Football Playoff in 2025, he will get another chance in 2027.

Texas A&M has invested a lot of money in football, and they expect returns. They have also been patient with coaches in the past. Kevin Sumlin lasted six seasons before diminishing returns led to him being let go. Jimbo Fisher also got six years before being shown the door. Mike Elko is in year three with Texas A&M. Still, Sumlin and Fisher never had the high of Elko, or the drop-off. After an 8-5 first season, the Aggies went 11-2 in 2025 with a loss in the first round of the College Football Playoff. Despite being 11-2 in 2025, the end of the season was a disappointment. They were 11-0 before losing to Texas in the final game of the year, and losing their chance to play in the SEC Championship game. They then fell to Miami in the first round of the playoffs.

This year, Texas A&M could miss a bowl game. They opened up 2-0 with wins over Missouri State and Arizona State, but have since lost six of their last eight games. The only wins for Texas A&M have been over Arkansas and The Citadel. Losing to Oklahoma and Texas to end the season would mean a 4-8 season, their worst since 2008. The offense has been dreadful, l eading to Elko apologizing for the team . It also sounded like a plea to keep his job.

"An utter apology with everything that I have to everybody that supports this program. Thank you for turning out. You deserve so much better. Give me a chance, and we will get this fixed, and we put a much better product on the field," Elko said.

If the Aggies go from the playoffs and contender in the SEC to last place in the conference, Elko may not get the chance to turn things around.

Washington went 9-4 after winning the LA Bowl in 2025. It was an improvement on the 6-7 first season Fisch had at Washington. The Huskies entered the season ranked 17th in the AP Poll, bringing back nearly two-thirds of the roster, and expected to contend in the Big Ten while pushing for the playoffs. Washington is not contending this year. After a 3-0 start, they dropped their first three games in conference play. Two of the losses included second-half collapses and clock management blunders by the coaching staff. Now, Washington is 6-4, but with games against Indiana and Oregon still on deck, a 6-6 finish is likely.

F isch has already been questioned by the fan base multiple times this year, and the regression from last year to this season will lead to more calls for his job. Fisch flirted with other jobs at the end of last year as well, including being linked to the Michigan job. His wandering eye is remembered by fans and could intensify calls for his job. With a $25 million buyout, a mutual parting of ways may be more likely, but if Fisch survives, he will enter 2027 on the hot seat.

Unless there is a major reason to get rid of a coach after just one year, it normally does not happen. Major reasons could include some type of impropriety or even a coach bolting for a better job. The other reason would be a complete collapse, which is what is going on at Tulane. Willie Fritz built Tulane into a conference title and CFP contender. He led them to a Cotton Bowl win and a 12-2 record in 2022. The next year, Tulane lost in their conference title game to SMU but still finished 11-3. Fritz moved on to Houston, and Jon Sumrall took over. Sumrall brought Tulane back to the American Conference title game his first year, losing to Army and finishing 9-5. Last year, Tulane reached the conference title game for a fourth straight season, winning it and earning a spot in the College Football Playoff.

The expectation was for Tulane to continue to excel in the conference. Instead, they will be hoping to just make a bowl in their first year under Will Hall. They are 5-5 and have been blown out multiple times, including a 42-19 loss at home to UTSA and a 60-10 loss, also at home, to Tulsa. Tulane will be an underdog in their last two games and could miss a bowl for the first time since 2021.

This is also not a new name to the program, so the university may already know what they have. He was the offensive coordinator under Fritz in 2019 and 2020 before becoming the Southern Miss head coach. He went just 14-30 there before being fired. Then, last year he came back as the passing game coordinator and was able to keep many key players from the playoff team. That makes the season look even worse and could lead to Hall losing his job.

One of the signs that a coach may be in danger is when he starts reshuffling his assistants in an effort to keep his job. Oftentimes, it's like reshuffling chairs on the Titanic. It does not matter where you put them; the ship is going down. Jeff Lebby let go of two coaches over the weekend as the season has gone south. Mississippi State started 4-0, and Kamario Taylor was a potential Heisman candidate.

Then, Alabama happened. Alabama beat Mississippi State 56-23 in Starkville. Taylor was injured in the game and has thrown just five passes since. Meanwhile, Mississippi State has lost six straight. Only one game has been tight, a two-point loss at home to Vanderbilt. Lebby is now 11-24 as the head coach of Mississippi State. The Bulldogs should get a win this weekend against Tennessee Tech, but an Egg Bowl loss to Ole Miss could end his tenure. The one thing that could save Lebby is Mississippi State trying to keep Taylor from transferring .

Dabo Swinney has already been on the hot seat rankings before , and continues to sit on them now. Clemson was once dominant under Swinney, making the playoffs six straight years, and winning two national titles. Now, there has been regression. He has made the playoffs just once since the 2020 berth, and last year went 7-6. This year, Clemson is 6-4 and was just eliminated from contention in the ACC. Clemson lost to Georgia Tech on Saturday, 20-6. It was just the third win of the season for Georgia Tech.

Making matters worse, the roster construction for Swinney's squad is being exposed. Tait Reynolds, the freshman quarterback, will be out for the rest of the year . Meanwhile, Christopher Vizzina has been injured and ineffective. Trent Pearman also got time against Georgia Tech and had just six yards passing. With no one to turn to at quarterback, Clemson could be exposed against Duke and South Carolina, which would end up in a 6-6 season. It would be their worst season since 2010, and may lead to the end of the Swinney era at Clemson.

Sometimes, coaches just become stale at one place. Sometimes, a coach is just not a good fit in a certain place. Rarely is it both. That is the case with Lance Leipold at Kansas. Leipold was a quarterback at Wisconsin-Whitewater in college in the 1980s. He then got his first coaching job at Wisconsin-Whitewater in 1987 as the quarterback coach. He would slowly move up the coaching ranks until becoming the head coach at Wisconsin-Whitewater in 2007. In eight seasons, he led the Warhawks to six Division III Championships and a loss in one championship game.

Leipold then moved to Buffalo. He took the Bulls to three bowl games, two conference title games, and a Top 25 ranking to end the 2020 season. It was the first time that Buffalo had finished a season ranked in program history. In 2021, he took over Kansas. In that time, Kansas has not finished better than tied for seventh in the Big 12. They have been to two bowl games and had just one winning season, coming in 2023. Kansas has been ranked in the AP Top 25 a combined nine weeks in the six years of Leipold, with five of those weeks coming in 2023. They opened 2024 ranked 22nd, but dropped quickly after a 1-5 start.

Leipold is 31-41 all-time at Kansas, and 4-6 this year. With games against BYU and Oklahoma State to end the season, Kansas is likely to miss a bowl game for a third straight season. With Leipold being 62 years old, he may choose retirement over termination, but the time has come for Kansas to move on from Leipold.

Bo Schembechler was hired as the head coach in 1969 and led Michigan to an 8-3 record with a Rose Bowl appearance in his first year. In 1990, Gary Moeller took over. He went 9-3 with a win in the Gator Bowl and a top-ten finish. In 1995, Lloyd Carr was hired after Moeller was forced to resign. Carr led Michigan to a 9-4 season and a top-25 ranking. Brady Hoke also found success in his first season in 2011, finishing 11-2 with a Sugar Bowl win and finishing ranked in the top 15. Jim Harbaugh in 2015 also went 10-2, finishing ranked 12th. Even Sherrone Moore finished 8-5.

The only coach not to have success in their first year since 1969 was Rich Rodriguez, who went 3-9 in 2008. This means that in the last seven hires for Michigan before Kyle Whittingham, six of them finished with a winning record, five of them finished ranked, and four of them likely would have made a 12-team playoff. Then, there is Whittingham.

It is a different situation from Rodriguez. Rich Rod inherited a roster that was completely contrary to his style of play, with no transfer portal or NIL. It was known it would take time to make things right. Whittingham has the transfer portal, and while he got a slightly late start due to when Moore was fired, he still has a roster that should be winning more games. Michigan is 5-5 this year and needed a miracle to beat Western Michigan, plus beat Rutgers by just seven. With games against UCLA and Ohio State left, Whittingham may miss a bowl and lose his job. Still, winning one of the final two could change the outlook for his future.

articles.title: Monday Night Football: Chargers lead Ravens 17-10 at halftime
articles.summary: Justin Herbert and Omarion Hampton have touchdown runs for the winless Chargers.
articles.body:
The Chargers lead the Ravens 17-10 at halftime on Monday. That is more points than the winless Chargers have scored in five games and the same as they scored in a 23-17 loss to the Broncos.

They scored 23 against Seattle and 22 last week against Houston.

Los Angeles scored on 3-of-5 first-half possessions, getting a 22-yard touchdown run from Justin Herbert, a 38-yard Cameron Dicker field goal and a 1-yard Omarion Hampton touchdown run.

Hampton's touchdown came on fourth-and-goal with 1:56 remaining in the half. Roquan Smith initially had Hampton stopped before the running back got a push from offensive lineman Cole Strange and a pull from fullback Scott Matlock. Officials should have penalized Matlock for the pull, as pulling is illegal.

The Chargers outgained the Ravens 175 to 161, with Baltimore having no rushing yards on six carries.

Herbert, who injured his left hand in last week's loss to the Texans but wasn't on the injury report this week, went 6-for-9 for 91 yards in the first half. He also ran for 45 yards on six carries.

Hampton has 36 yards on 10 carries, and Tre' Harris has five catches for 86 yards.

Jacoby Brissett, making his first start for the Ravens after the trade from Arizona, has completed 14 of 23 passes for 163 yards and an interception. Del'Shawn Phillips had the pick on a pass that was behind Ja'Kobi Lane and deflected to the Chargers linebacker.

Derrick Henry has a 2-yard touchdown run, but he has minus-1 yard on five carries. Mark Andrews has four catches for 41 yards.

articles.summary: Después de su exhibición en el Metropolitano, el inglés parece estar de regreso al punto de influencia en el juego que demostró en sus primeros meses con el Real Madrid
articles.body: Pocos futbolistas tuvieron un impacto tan extraordinario en LaLiga. Sobre todo en el Real Madrid, donde en su momento se llegó a discutir si Zidane valía para el club. Zidane. Cuidado. Bellingham se acercó más a Ronaldo Nazario, que marcó a los pocos segundos del debut. El inglés deslumbró durante cuatro meses largos, con exhibición incluida en El Clásico. Jude ‘zidaneaba’, gobernaba el juego y decidía partidos. Pero en noviembre de 2023, ante el Rayo, cayó en mala postura y todo se torció. El hombro y una progresión asombrosa. El daño en el labrum izquierdo fue mucho más serio de lo que pareció aquel día en el Bernabéu. Porque poco a poco fue perdiendo presencia en el campo, ocultando bajo la camiseta un vendaje aparatoso para minimizar el dolor. Los datos disimularon el bajón. Antes de la caída sumó diez goles y dos asistencias en Liga, tres y dos en Champions. Después, nueve goles y cuatro asistencias en Liga, un gol y cuatro asistencias en Champions, incluida la de la final a Vinicius. Los números cayeron algo en su segunda campaña, 15 goles y 15 asistencias en 58 partidos, incluyendo los del Mundial de Clubes, ya con Xabi Alonso en el banquillo. Pero el bajón definitivo se produjo en el pasado ejercicio, al que se incorporó tarde tras operarse de la articulación maldita. Apenas ocho goles y cinco asistencias en 40 partidos. Tampoco jugaron a favor del futbolista de Birmingham las insinuaciones de su rendimiento fuera del campo. La celebración del gol ante el Mónaco, empinando el codo, respondió a los cuchicheos. Tiene gracia el apodo de Jude Ballantines cuando sus iniciales son JB. Cuestión de paladar. El Mundial ha devuelto la versión 1.0 de Bellingham. La exhibición en el Metropolitano con Inglaterra no es un accidente. Dijo Mourinho que se ponía enfermo al verle defender como un central en años anteriores, que le quería cerca del área. A él le da igual. Aparece en todos los sectores, desde el origen de la jugada al desenlace. En 16 partidos con el Real Madrid, cinco goles, cuatro asistencias y la convicción de que Jude vuelve a ‘zidanear’. PD. Semana 194. Dimisiones, 0; ceses, 0. La jueza del Caso Negreira está a punto de decidir si abre juicio o lo da por sobreseído. La evidencia es que el Barcelona pagó a Enríquez Negreira, vicepresidente de los árbitros en ejercicio, y su hijo durante casi dos décadas. Y nadie ha asumido la responsabilidad de una inmoralidad semejante.

articles.title: Vuelve Vinicius... y ¿ahora qué, Mou?
articles.summary: Una opinión de Roberto Gómez
articles.body: Después de cumplir la exagerada sanción de cuatro partidos y tras los compromisos con la selección con Brasil del cuestionado Ancelotti, y en los que el ‘7’ fue de los pocos jugadores de la Canarinha que se han salvado, Vinicius, el gran Vinicius, vuelve a estar a disposición de Mourinho también en liga. ¿Y ahora qué? Qué pasará ahora con un futbolista madridista de verdad, implicado como pocos en defender y partirse la cara por su equipo, aspirante a ser el mejor del mundo, que fue clave para que el Real Madrid conquistara Champions, ligas... que tuvo ofertas por las que casi la totalidad de los profesionales no las hubieran rechazado y se prefirió quedarse en el club blanco por menos dinero que le ofrecían y firmando un contrato de seis años que le presentó Florentino Pérez y quien, de momento, no le ha defendido en público, pero que no estaría nada mal que lo hiciese. Mou lo tiene claro y muy claro, titularisimo. Pero habrá que esperar a los entrenamientos y a otro factor importante, el de los aficionados que de una manera sorprendente, además de decepcionante, que han pasado de considerarle un ídolo intocable a criticarle como pocas veces se ha visto en la historia del Real Madrid. Vinicius vuelve. Ahora hay que esperar la decisión de Mourinho. El futuro no lo tiene claro el astro brasileño. Luis de la Fuente entregará una camiseta firmada por la selección española a Morante de la Puebla. El seleccionador recibio el pasado 12 de octubre un vestido de torear del diestro sevillano en una reunión organizada por el empresario Rafael García Garrido. El seleccionador le entregará una camiseta que a Morante le hace muchísima ilusión. El próximo 23 de abril se celebrará la Gala del Arbitraje, que estará presidida por Fran Soto, el máximo responsable del CTA. Durante la gala se premiará a los mejores árbitros españoles de todas las categorías tanto de las ligas profesionales, LaLiga y Segunda, como de las categorías del fútbol aficionado español.

articles.title: Mario Balotelli: Why always him? The rise and fall of the Italian striker
articles.summary: Fifteen years since his 'Why always me?' Manchester derby T-shirt celebration, BBC Sport looks at the career of former Manchester City striker Mario Balotelli.
articles.body:
Perhaps better known for off-field antics than his undeniable - yet arguably wasted - talent with the ball at his feet, the Italian has always attracted headlines.

Fifteen years have passed since his famous 'Why always me?' Manchester derby T-shirt celebration, which came just days after a firework was set off in his own bathroom, causing a house fire.

The 36-year-old is still playing, now in the United Arab Emirates first division with Al-Ittifaq alongside his biological brother, Enock Barwuah.

Here, BBC Sport looks at a career that has included 13 clubs, six countries - and an assist for arguably the most famous goal in Premier League history.

Mancini to Mourinho - cracks begin to show

Typical of his unconventional footballing life, Balotelli's career did not begin in an elite club's academy.

Instead, by his mid-teens he was turning out for Italian third-tier side Lumezzane, close to the family home in Concesio.

A trial at Barcelona did not lead to a long-term stay, and instead he was picked up by Inter Milan in 2006.

It was at Inter that Balotelli first came across his great mentor - Roberto Mancini.

The relationship between the two has been likened to that of a father and son. Under the Italian coach's tutelage, Balotelli flourished.

Aged 17, Balotelli helped Inter win the 2007-08 Serie A title and reach the Coppa Italia final, memorably scoring twice against Juventus to send his side into the semi-finals.

Life changed for Balotelli with the arrival of Jose Mourinho in the weeks after that campaign ended.

There would be disagreements, disciplinary action and accusations that Balotelli's attitude was not up to scratch. Mourinho said Balotelli was "unmanageable" and described one performance as "close to a zero rating".

The relationship with Mourinho was fractious - a rare occasion when the Special One was confounded by a player.

Balotelli still won three Serie A titles and one Champions League with Inter, but his reputation as a supposed loose cannon was already beginning to overshadow his feats as a player.

Logic dictated that Balotelli's next step should be to reunite with mentor Mancini. That happened in August 2010 when the 20-year-old joined Manchester City .

Mancini set out to show that the unpredictable ways of Balotelli could be harnessed for the team's good, aiming to get more out of him than Mourinho could.

A hardline stance on discipline often appeared to soften when Mancini dealt with Balotelli, who by spring 2011 had garnered a reputation in England as a fantastic footballer who could not stay away from controversy.

Having already been sent off twice for City and been involved in a car crash - not in his famous camouflage Bentley but an Audi R8 - the striker threw a dart at a youth-team player, an act that showed a level of immaturity.

After helping City to win the FA Cup in 2011, ending their 35-year major trophy drought, Balotelli came under scrutiny after attempting a backheel trick shot when through on goal during a pre-season friendly against LA Galaxy.

Mancini swiftly hooked him, later questioning his mentality by saying: "If you are serious, you can play 90 minutes. If not, you can come and sit by me on the bench."

Sometimes the audacity paid off - like the famous shoulder goal and subsequent nonchalant celebration against Norwich.

In October 2011, emergency services attended his Cheshire home to deal with a firework lit in his bathroom. Balotelli said a friend had been responsible.

BBC Sport reported at the time that four firefighters used two hose reel water jets to douse the flames, with a large fan deployed to clear smoke.

Days later he was in the spotlight for the right reasons as he scored City's opener in a 6-1 win over Manchester United , celebrating with the 'Why always me?' T-shirt.

There were other stories - that he had given a homeless person £1,000, that he had turned up to a young boy's school to confront the headmaster about the child being bullied, that he drove around Manchester handing out presents while dressed as Santa.

True? Perhaps only Balotelli knows and he has often denied such rumours. But such was his reputation at the time that the stories became plausible.

A chant City fans coined made reference to his ironic allergy to grass - which kept him out of a Europa League match in 2011 - and driving around Moss Side with "a wallet full of cash".

On the pitch, Balotelli was sent off against Arsenal in April 2012 in what, at the time, seemed like a season-defining moment that could end Manchester City 's title bid.

But one month later he assisted Sergio Aguero's last-gasp goal against Queens Park Rangers that gave City a first Premier League title. It was his only Premier League assist that season.

Micah Richards, who was a team-mate and friend to Balotelli at City, said: "He was crazy in a good way. He was brilliant to have around the squad - a cult hero not just for the nonsense he did off the field but on it as well.

"The best thing about him is he's a lovely guy - he's not arrogant or how the papers try to perceive him, he's just a bit mad."

But did the moments of brilliance make the "nonsense" worth it?

Despite once insisting his patience with Balotelli was "limitless", Mancini ultimately had a rethink.

The final straw came in January 2013 when the pair had an argument at the training ground. Balotelli left for AC Milan later that month.

Mancini said: "He is not a bad guy, and a fantastic player, but I'm very sorry for him as he continues to lose his talent and his quality. I don't have any words for his behaviour.

"I hope for him he can understand he is in a bad way for his future."

Affection remained on both sides, but the relationship had become too fraught.

"Once upon a time, Mario did genuinely believe he was one of the best players in the world," said Nedum Onuoha, another former City team-mate.

"There are lots of stories about him from his time at City, but the one I remember is at our old training ground in Carrington when someone was talking about Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, and Mario said he was as good as them - and he was deadly serious.

"It obviously hasn't worked out that way, but he still has done so much more with his career than most players could even dream of."

Mancini & Balotelli 'bust-up' Published 3 January 2013

'Balotelli to Barnsley? Now that is one Mario story I don't believe'

Balotelli never threatened to have an international career to rival Ronaldo or Messi.

But there were still moments that linger in the memory.

He became the first black player to feature for Italy at a major tournament when he starred at Euro 2012.

And, more than that, he hit three goals to finish as the tournament's joint top scorer - with five others - as Italy lost to Spain in the final.

An abiding image is that of a shirtless Balotelli flexing his muscles after scoring the goal that sent the Azzurri to the final, with a 2-1 win against Germany.

Yet that tournament proved to be the peak of Balotelli's international career.

Italy's national team took a downward turn, and so too did his club career. By 2015, Balotelli had more or less became an Azzurri afterthought.

While Balotelli enjoyed some big moments in an Italy shirt, he did not always feel the love reciprocated from his country of birth.

Before Euro 2012 he threatened to leave the pitch if he was subjected to racist abuse and spoke openly about the vitriol he suffered while playing for Inter.

In fact, racist abuse has followed Balotelli throughout his career and he has commendably refused to tolerate it.

Born Mario Barwuah in Palermo to Ghanaian parents, Balotelli was placed into foster care aged three.

Initially, he stayed with his foster parents - Silvia and Francesco Balotelli - in Brescia during the week, then returned to his biological parents at weekends. He was eventually fostered on a full-time basis and took on the Balotelli surname.

Balotelli identifies with both parts of his heritage - Ghana and Italy - and he struggled to reconcile his love for a nation with the people who aimed verbal abuse his way.

The good times were all too brief: 36 caps and 14 goals has been his tally since 2018. He wanted more and has often made it known.

Onuoha said: "Playing for his country was always so important to him and that's another really positive thing about him, that he had that drive and ambition."

Mancini told AC Milan that Balotelli could become one of the world's best while in Serie A.

A glut of goals followed the striker's return to the San Siro in January 2013, before a surprising move back to the Premier League followed 18 months later.

Liverpool had been impressed, but Balotelli's spell on Merseyside would prove forgettable for all. One goal in 16 Premier League games under Brendan Rodgers was not what was expected from the £16m buy.

The failed transfer sparked a loan move back to Milan, where injuries hampered his progress. When it was time for Balotelli to return to Merseyside, Jurgen Klopp had arrived and said the striker would not be part of his Liverpool plans.

Balotelli later called the move to Anfield "the worst mistake of my life".

Was it that Liverpool move that sent Balotelli's career spiralling into freefall?

Spells in Nice, Marseille, Brescia and Monza followed - each to varying degrees of success but never with a feeling of stability.

Then came Turkish club Adana Demirspor, Swiss outfit Sion and Italian side Genoa. He spent no more than one season at a time with any of these clubs, although he did return to Demirspor for a second stint.

And so to the present day, with Balotelli aged 36 and plying his trade in the UAE.

It is easy to wonder what might have been had Balotelli stayed in Manchester, had he managed to settle enough to entirely fulfil his potential.

But, after so much media attention and a career that has spanned more continents and leagues than most, it is perhaps also understandable that Balotelli has settled on fulfilment through simply playing the game he loves with his brother.

"Playing with a family member like he is will give him that happiness," said Onuoha.

"And yes, it is not Serie A, La Liga or the Premier League, but Mario is on a field sharing it with his brother - for him that will mean everything.

"At this point there aren't many people that would hold much against him. I think when he was younger, some people would.

"But now I think it is more a case of almost allowing him this happiness, and enjoying seeing him finish off the last days of his career in a place that makes him happy.

"So many people end their careers on a sour note, but for him he is going to be ending it doing exactly what he wants to do."

articles.title: Ronaldo, Maradona, Baggio - what happened to the World XI?
articles.summary: Football's biggest stars used to turn out in their prime for the Rest of the World XI, something that would not seem possible today.
articles.body:
Soren Colding wasn't expecting the call. "The Laudrup brothers, Peter Schmeichel, there might have been some cancellations," he jokes.

Eventually, the Danish FA turned to a Brondby defender who had played a handful of times for the national team.

The assignment? He would be expected to mark Ronaldo and Gabriel Batistuta as part of a Europe XI against the Rest of the World at Marseille's Velodrome.

It was December 1997, and Colding's team-mates would include defenders Fernando Hierro and Alessandro Costacurta, a midfield duo of Zinedine Zidane and Paul Ince, and Patrick Kluivert and Alen Boksic up top.

This was a star-sprinkled cast - one player from each of the competing nations at the following summer's World Cup joining forces before the draw took place.

"Of course, when you see those names, it was just more or less a dream come true," explains the Dane.

Colding was flown to France and chauffeured to the hotel. His driver offered to hang around in case the full-back fancied an impromptu shopping trip. There was no need. Instead, he discovered a bag of Fifa goodies in his room.

"There was the biggest Adidas bag I have ever seen in my life," he smiles. "I found a training suit and went down to lunch.

"Then I saw all the other guys on round tables - they were sitting with their agents, their wives, their family, their friends in normal [clothes]. Then the Danish guy turned in. Nobody knows who he is, in his Adidas training suit!"

Colding struck up a friendship with South Africa defender David Nyathi and the pair were whisked off to a 45-minute training session that afternoon. Not all the big names took part, but one Argentine offered a taste of what was to come.

"Batistuta was there and just to see him and his moves, you thought, 'Okay, it's gonna be a nice evening tomorrow'," remembers Colding, who also got to link up with European boss Franz Beckenbauer.

"He was pretty cool. He was saying, 'what is your position? Defender? OK, can you play left defender?' No problem - I'll play wherever you place me!"

Come game day, 38,000 fans packed in to see peak Ronaldo. Months earlier, Il Fenomeno completed a world-record move to Inter Milan on the back of 47 goals in 49 games in one sensational season at Barcelona.

The 21-year-old was the most exciting player on the planet.

"It was crazy, actually," recalls Colding, who previously faced the forward when Denmark's under-21s played Brazil in Florianopolis before the 1996 Olympics.

"That was almost the same team as they played with at the World Cup in '98. So we lost 5-1. Just to see his speed and how he played - I played against Roberto Carlos in that game as well - that was just another level. I thought, 'what is going on here?'

"When I saw him there again, it was just to see what is actually reachable for a football player, because that was next level tremendous. His speed and his touch are unbelievable, and also his power.

"And still, just a small, shy guy. You know, he just wants to play football, and all these people are around him protecting him. Just to see when a star like him joins an event like that, how many people around him, agents and followers, how should you navigate all that?"

Ronaldo, captaining Carlos Alberto Parreira's side, was at his blistering best, scoring twice and setting up the other three as Rest of the World won 5-2 - Batistuta also netted twice, before Zidane responded.

"You start thinking what if you injured some of them," explains Colding. "You are a defender, you don't want goals against you, so you have to fight - that's how I am.

"How hard should you go to them? Should you just let them go? No. I would not just let them run and score. I tried to do my best, that was probably not good enough!"

This wasn't the first outing for a World XI, in fact such Fifa exhibition matches had been taking place since England hosted an all-star side in front of a reported 100,000 fans at Wembley in 1963 to celebrate the Football Association's centenary.

They became a semi-regular occurrence as testimonials or charity fixtures, with huge names appearing across eras from Eusebio and Zico to Roberto Baggio.

But the biggest coup was arguably luring Diego Maradona to Wembley a year after winning the World Cup with Argentina and scoring his 'Hand of God' goal against England.

Jon Smith, who represented the Napoli star, explains in his book 'The Deal' how Maradona was offered around £250,000 and flown from Naples on a private jet to take part in an anniversary game against the Football League.

"In fairness, he wanted to shake hands with the team and say 'sorry if I offended you'," Smith tells BBC Sport. "He genuinely believed his talent was God-given.

"He was sort of two people. He was lovely, Diego, when you were with him. When he crossed the white line he was Maradona. So the Hand of God was an expression of 'I am God's footballing representative', if you like.

"It was madness, because you can imagine how the media were all over it. It was a bit special."

Napoli and Argentina welcomed the opportunity for Maradona to generate some good PR in England, helped by Bobby Robson's Football League side winning 3-0 - Bryan Robson netting twice and Norman Whiteside grabbing the other.

"I remember introducing him to Bobby Robson," adds Smith. "He put his hand out, and Bobby said 'I'm not shaking that hand!', which I thought was lovely - he did shake the other hand!"

One of the final games saw a Ronaldinho XI take on a Shevchenko XI at Nou Camp in February 2005 to raise funds for victims of the 2004 tsunami.

Andriy Shevchenko's stacked squad included Zidane, David Beckham, Alessandro Del Piero, Thierry Henry, Raul, Paolo Maldini and Steven Gerrard.

Ronaldinho could call on Ronaldo, Kaka, Cafu, Adriano, Javier Zanetti, Didier Drogba and Samuel Eto'o, though it was Southampton's Henri Camara who scored twice in a 6-3 win for the Brazilian's team.

But things have moved on, and it is hard to imagine clubs releasing their star players for such an exhibition nowadays.

"The whole world of football has changed," says Smith. "You used to have testimonial games and testimonial years because players got paid okay but by the same token weren't earning £100k a week.

"It wouldn't happen now because the business of football is so much bigger, you can't risk the players - if they get injured playing for their country, that annoys everybody.

"But beyond that they are owned by big corporations and in some cases countries, so you just wouldn't allow your player to go out and do that."

Colding went on to play 27 times for Denmark, featuring at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000, but retains fond memories of representing the Europe XI.

"Now, to come up with the idea to make a game like this, in combination with the draw, I think everyone will say you are crazy," explains Colding.

"But at that time it was perfectly planned and a fantastic event to be a part of. As players, we have a tremendous relationship between each other.

"It shows all the spectators you can be enemies on the field, but you can actually be friends and gather together in this kind of event.

"That for me sends a signal to all that we are a community in football and we can actually make great things together that not only is a question of money."

In fact, he still has his Europe shirt - a reminder of coming up against Ronaldo and Batistuta and being a team-mate of Zidane almost 30 years ago.

"It doesn't smell very good, actually," laughs Colding. "Sometimes, when I go in the garage with my kids and tell them about it and what actually happened, I see in their eyes, they don't really believe that I was a part of that game.

"That was not about money - we didn't get anything to join - it was just because you represent your country, so it was a great experience, it's also about having fun.

"You know, as small kids, you don't start by saying, 'I want to earn 20 million'. No, you start because it's fun to play football."

articles.title: Nations League: Are Scotland still too reliant on 'old guard'?
articles.summary: After a bruising defeat in Switzerland to conclude Scotland's Nations League campaign, questions are being asked about the direction of travel under new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli.
articles.body:
As Zeki Amdouni arrowed in second-string Switzerland's fabulous fourth goal, the body language of dejected Scotland duo Andy Robertson and Ryan Christie was telling.

The captain's record-breaking 103rd cap played out in cruel fashion. Suited and booted for the occasion, with commemorative boots and a personalised armband, there was no cause for celebration as Robertson was, yet again, wheeled out afterwards to make sense of the 4-0 scudding in St Gallen.

So too were John McGinn and Kieran Tierney. Billy Gilmour, who has also surpassed the half-century caps landmark, also did a bit of talking. Substitute Christie was spared this time.

After a result of this kind, rounding up a humdrum maiden campaign for manager Sebastien Pocognoli, it's necessary for the experienced heads to front-up.

When he named his first squad, so much kudos was thrown the Belgian's way for breaking away from the norm and bleeding in the stars of tomorrow.

But such young and bright lights were only allowed to shine on the bench, at best, as Pocognoli turned to the tried and tested.

As former Scotland international Leanne Crichton said on BBC Scotland's Sportscene: "There's a reliance still, clearly, on that key core of Scotland players.

"And, when you listen to it post-match, they sound dejected, they don't sound that confident about what is going on. It is a difficult place to be."

Pocognoli's abject Scotland suffer 4-0 Nations League defeat in Switzerland

St Gallen was a mighty troubling place for the Scots on Monday night.

The calm, picturesque city was invaded by coral shirt and kilt-clad Scotsmen from Sunday, but they - and their heroes on the pitch - couldn't wait to get out of the place after a poor showing at the Sitterstadion.

A narrow half-time deficit turned into a drubbing on the final whistle, at which the Scots remained goalless despite a handful of hopeful situations.

McGinn, the scorer of Scotland's past three goals, directed a weak header goalbound before the break, while Scott McTominay - nearly one year on from his Hampden heroics against Denmark - missed a couple of glaring opportunities.

"If McTominay is not operating at his highest level for the national team, there is an impact on results," Crichton said.

"If McGinn doesn't produce the goods on an evening, we're in trouble.

"If Gilmour and Ferguson in the middle of the pitch [don't perform], if Christie doesn't come on with an impact, we are [too reliant].

"And that's where you need to breed a different confidence in a different group."

Kieron Bowie, who many hoped would be in from the off, came on just before the hour mark and got right in about it, as is the striker's style.

Winger Ben Gannon-Doak, dropped for Aaron Hickey, did come on after the wing-back ended up going off with an apparent hamstring injury before Kristi Montgomery was handed a debut with five minutes to go.

Wide-men Findlay Curtis and Josh McPake were left on the bench, again. Robbie Ure didn't make either matchday squad this camp.

All three natural wingers excite supporters, even if they have only been handed a matter of minutes, but Pocognoli's system does not suit them.

That said, the players insist they're invested in the project.

"We have to believe that we're going in the right direction," Robertson added after a beyond-deflating defeat.

"Of course, there's going to be humps in the road, but when I look back on Steve Clarke's opening six games - I can't remember all the results but - I don't think everyone was shouting and screaming about Steve Clarke's Scotland after the first six games.

"We're trying to get a team together and we're trying to build a good atmosphere off the pitch.

"People wanted change within the squad. We've done that change and now we need to try and integrate the squad.

"We need to get close as a squad again, integrate the young players, make them feel a part of it, make them step up - it's for us to try and help them do it."

articles.title: Scotland: What’s going wrong for head coach Sebastien Pocognoli and can he turn things around?
articles.summary: Scotland ended their Nations League campaign with a 4-0 defeat to Switzerland; Sebastien Pocognoli has won two of his first six games as head coach; the Scots are set to find themselves in pot three for next month's Euro 2028 qualifying draw
articles.body:
From a historic night against Denmark as the long wait to return to the World Cup finally ended, to a bruising 4-0 defeat to Switzerland at the end of a frustrating Nations League campaign. The contrast is stark.

A second-half collapse against a second-string Swiss side in St Gallen condemned the Scots to their heaviest loss since their 5-1 thrashing by Germany at Euro 2024.

After also leading Scotland to back-to-back Euros, Steve Clarke was always going to be a hard act to follow. After just six games, some of the Tartan Army have already seen enough from Sebastien Pocognoli.

The new head coach managed two wins against North Macedonia in Group B1. The third-place finish means Scotland will be in pot three when the qualifying draw is made for Euro 2028 on December 6, meaning a potentially more challenging campaign.

Pocognoli wants time, something even his captain Andy Robertson said you do not get in international football.

What is going wrong for the new head coach?

Pocognoli has consistently stressed the need for patience as he tries to implement a more attack-minded style.

He favours a back three featuring wing-backs, with two attacking midfielders or a central playmaker supporting a single striker as he looks to press high up the pitch.

The issue is, Scotland don't have the right players.

Pacy winger Ben Gannon-Doak has frequently been deployed at right wing-back in this system, but his natural attacking fair is being limited by the defensive demands that brings.

While Clarke did use a back five in his early tenure to try and accomodate both Andy Roberston and John McGinn, he favoured a more traditional back four.

His teams were not always entertaining to watch, but they did get the job done. Most of the time.

The question for Pocognoli is, should he stick to his principles or look at what his predecessor did to bring the highs the Tartan Army had been missing?

After two camps and six games, any grace period the Belgian had is over.

Time with the players is something international managers do not have, but Pocognoli has already had more than some.

The elongated international window between September and October, followed by the most recent camp means he has had 24 days with his squad. That is equivalent to what a Scottish Premiership side has between day one of pre-season and their first game in the League Cup group stages.

Andy Robertson became Scotland's most capped men's player against Switzerland, but there was not much for the captain to celebrate.

"That cannot happen in international football," he told BBC Scotland after the match.

"I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it. These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden, who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.

"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up."

John McGinn echoed his skipper when asked if Scotland were on the right path: "Well, obviously the trajectory of the results means it's impossible for me to say yes."

James Scott from the Football Park Scotland podcast speaking on Sky Sports News:

"It's the early days and the players. It'll take time for us to maybe get going on this but that can't be the detriment of results.

"We can accept a poor performance against Macedonia, still getting the win, but coming away against Switzerland, it's a much tougher task and I think we could save face a bit by maybe just making a few adjustments.

"Losing against Switzerland is not a bad thing but to ship four goals in the manner we did with the lack of fight, the jury's out on the formation now. It's starting to frustrate people.

"We've got two friendlies now in March, Euro qualifiers starting next year. If things don't change in the friendlies, the frustration really will start to build because you don't get a lot of time in international football and I think mistakes do cost you more.

"We can't make amends for last night until then and then the qualifiers come around and there's really no room to slip up there because you don't want to be relying on the sort of safety net of being a host to get in.

"We would like to qualify and we don't want to miss out on a tournament that's happening in our own back garden and not being there."

The next international break is not until March, with two friendlies before the Euro 2028 qualifying campaign kicks off.

Robertson admitted the long wait is "not a good thing" as they look to regroup after the Nations League disappointment.

While that means no time on the pitch with his players, Pocognoli will have time to assess his squad and tactics. If the Scottish FA decides he is still the right man to lead the national team to their next major tournament.

articles.title: Tony Mowbray steps down as Blackburn Rovers head coach due to health issues
articles.summary: Tony Mowbray has stepped down from his role as Blackburn Rovers head coach due to health issues.
articles.body:
The 62-year-old returned to football at West Brom last year following his recovery from bowel cancer, before taking charge at Blackburn in June.

In a statement, Mowbray said: "Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as head coach of Blackburn Rovers.

"I'm immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I've loved working with them.

"Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you've given me. It's been a pleasure working alongside you.

"To the fans, thank you for the way you've supported me and the team this season. I've always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me.

"I'm grateful to the owners and Suhail [Shaikh, Blackburn's chief operating officer] for giving me the opportunity to lead this great club once again.

"I'd ask that you give me and my family privacy at this time.

"Thank you for your understanding. Tony."

Mowbray had enjoyed an impressive start to his second spell at Blackburn. Tipped for relegation by many, Rovers currently sit just three points off the play-offs in 13th. In their last game before the international break they beat West Ham 2-1.

Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds will take charge of first-team affairs heading into Sunday's game with Burnley.

articles.title: Gregg Broughton interview: Chicago Fire sporting director on Robert Lewandowski and a club trying to find an edge in MLS
articles.summary: In this exclusive interview with Sky Sports, Chicago Fire sporting director Gregg Broughton discusses Robert Lewandowski's impact on and off the pitch and explains why he is just part of the grand plans to revitalise the football club as they prepare for the MLS play-offs...
articles.body:
Broughton is a 50-year-old Englishman who cut his teeth as academy boss at Luton and Norwich before moving to Bodo/Glimt and then becoming sporting director at Blackburn. His job now, with the help of Robert Lewandowski, is to help deliver it for Chicago Fire.

Things are looking promising. Last season, the team reached the play-offs for the first time in eight years. This time, they are back. "Two years in a row for the first time since 2009." But this is about more than results. Broughton is part of a massive project here.

There is already a new training ground. The stadium is next, a purpose-built arena that will open in the summer of 2028. "Every week it gets bigger as you drive past it. You can feel momentum building. It keeps everyone focused. We know where we want to be."

That means winning trophies rather than being perennial underachievers. Chicago Fire had long had a top-10 budget but not the results to match. That is changing and the headline-grabbing acquisition of Lewandowski is already proving more than symbolic.

Inevitably, there have been goals. Nine of them, including three in his last two games. But Broughton points to Lewandowski's wider impact. With a significant Polish community in Chicago, he has put thousands on the gate. And not just for home games.

"In Toronto and New York, you are seeing thousands with Poland shirts on, Chicago Fire shirts with Lewandowski on the back. There are enormous benefits off the field." On the field, it goes beyond his own performances. It is about how he influences others as well.

Broughton saw that up close when the academy players travelled with the team to an away game in New England. "They are all sat on the plane in absolute silence, scared to even lift their eyes up. He literally went up to every single person and shook their hand."

On the way back, Lewandowski sat next to the head coach. "The moment the plane was in the air, Robert was going through every single clip for an hour and a half because he is meticulous, not only about his own performance but the performance of the team too."

Broughton believes Lewandowski "is demonstrating what performance at the very highest level looks like" and his own job is help ensure that this is mirrored across the organisation. "We have a lot of resources," he admits. The difficulty is finding an edge.

The hope is that by investing in the infrastructure around the team they can get that "return on every single dollar" and that means being best in class in every department. Broughton highlights Darcy Norman, director of physical performance, as an example.

"He is a world-leading expert at the cutting edge of performance who has won the World Cup with Germany, the Champions League with Bayern Munich." Eddie Rock, the head of strategy, knows the "unique rules around roster building in MLS inside out" as well.

"We have the biggest analytics team in MLS," claims Broughton. Because while the signing of Lewandowski might not scream hidden gem, he was atypical. "We put a lot of weight on projection models, going into markets that might not traditionally sell to MLS."

Led by head of recruitment Michael Stephens, they picked up Dje D'Avilla. "An Ivorian player from the Portuguese second division." Mbekezeli Mbokazi, signed from Orlando Pirates, has been a revelation. "The highest-performing central defender in MLS."

The analytics played a key role here. "MLS has big imbalances in certain areas of the field," Broughton explains. "That means more turnovers, more transitions. And that puts more demand on the physical output. That is a really important piece of information."

What it also means is that by bringing in players from other competitions "where running is not as highly valued" it is possible for them to get more bang for their buck. "If you have good models, good eyes and you are clearly aligned, that gives you a chance."

It is striking how often Broughton seeks to give credit to his colleagues. He remembers his time at Blackburn where he was managing upwards with the ownership and then having to lead the other departments but responsibilities feel shared in Chicago.

Zayne Thomajan, the general manager, was instrumental in Lewandowski's move going so smoothly. "She completely drove the relocation plans with his family, bringing a major star into a foreign city and making sure that he could assimilate so quickly."

He notes that president Dave Baldwin had a key role. There were billboards set up in Chicago celebrating Lewandowski before he had even signed. "A business decision and a correct decision. It is about building a brand for these stars in the American market."

But one suspect that Broughton's own characteristics bring the best out in others too. He holds the UEFA Pro Licence despite not having coaching aspirations. That surely helps his relationship with Gregg Berhalter, the head coach and director of football.

"It allows me to sit there and have the football conversations with him, while also knowing that I am not after his job."

He has enough on his plate with his own, a role that involves defining the culture of the club. It was something he did to great effect at Bodo, playing his part in the rise of a previously obscure outfit from near the Arctic Circle to the top of Norwegian football.

"The mission statement there was to make the fans proud but what did that actually mean? Nobody had ever asked that before." In Chicago, he is on a similar fact-finding mission, trying to drill down into the essence of the place to discover what will resonate.

Are there any similarities between the two? "Both have brutal winters. I will never moan about England again," he jokes. "But Chicago is a hardworking industrial city without some of the airs and graces that you maybe get on the east or west coast of America."

Without the success too, but maybe that is about to change. "We want to compete for championships. We have been very open about that. Our job is to make Chicago Fire one of those topics that people are talking about in bars and restaurants in the city."

Starting with their play-off against Charlotte on Sunday.

articles.title: Gruda, el 'apadrinado' por Messi que destrozó a Xavi: "Es un jugador de clase mundial"
articles.standfirst: La nueva joya de Alemania fue seleccionada por Leo como "uno de los diez jóvenes más prometedores del fútbol mundial"
articles.summary: La nueva joya de Alemania fue seleccionada por Leo como "uno de los diez jóvenes más prometedores del fútbol mundial"
articles.body: En el día que Alemania decía adiós a Adidas después de 72 años, unas botas de la compañía fundada en 1949 por 'Adi' Dassler tuvieron mucho que decir, las de Brajan Gruda (Speyer, 2004). El 'playmaker' del Brighton, cedido actualmente en el RB Leipzig, destrozó a la Países Bajos de Xavi Hernández (5-0). El extremo derecho de la 'Mannschaft' marcó un gol y repartió dos asistencias para propinar a la 'Oranje' su peor derrota en 67 años. Hasta ahí todo normal... si no fuera porque Gruda forma parte del elenco de futbolistas 'apadrinados' por Leo Messi. El ex del Mainz recibió un par de botas 'F50 Vis10n' en octubre de 2025 después de ser identificado por el ex del Barcelona como "uno de los diez jóvenes más prometedores del fútbol mundial". "Soy un gran admirador de Messi. Es el mejor jugador de todos los tiempos. [Ser elegido] no es una carga, sino una gran motivación", reconocía Gruda, que, recientemente, recibió un nuevo 'pack' con las 'F50 Messi El Último Tango', las botas que el argentino 'calzó' en su despedida, coincidiendo con su partido número 208 con la 'Albiceleste'. "En honor a las 208 apariciones de [Messi] con la selección nacional, sólo se produjeron 208 pares en todo el mundo, uno de los cuales fue el que Leo usó en el terreno de juego. Algunos pares seleccionados de esta edición estrictamente limitada también fueron entregados a creadores de contenido, medios de comunicación y amigos y allegados de Messi", confesaba Oliver Brüggen, portavoz de Adidas, a 'Bild'. Lo curioso de Gruda es que es un recién llegado a la selección: sólo suma dos partidos con la absoluta. En su debut contra Serbia (1-3) dejó su sello con un golazo y un amplio abanico de regates: completó 9 de 14. Un registro que, según 'Opta', sólo ha superado Jamal Musiala (13) con Alemania en los últimos 10 años. En la 'manita' a Países Bajos volvió a vestirse de 'MVP para regocijo de Jürgen Klopp: "Dios mío, Scherhant y Gruda ¡saben jugar al fútbol de verdad! Pero, por si fuera poco, la cantidad de trabajo que meten es tremenda. Eso es lo que hace a un equipo. Muchos jugadores saben jugar al fútbol, pero se trata del esfuerzo, el compromiso y la pasión que le pones. Eso es lo que al final importa". En cambio, Bastian Schweinsteiger, en 'ARD', prefería poner el acento sobre su talento. "Es un sueño tener a jugadores como Wirtz, Scherhant o Gruda en el equipo. Son futbolistas que marcan la diferencia. Este último es de clase mundial". Una teoría sobre la que incidía 'Sport 1', que bautizó a Gruda y Wirtz como "dos maestros del balón". "Gruda fue, una vez más, el jugador con ese factor espectáculo tan característico, aunque también propenso a perder el balón en algunas ocasiones. Sin embargo, en general es una buena señal la audacia y la valentía con la que juega este joven de 22 años para la selección alemana, lo que hace que algún que otro error sea perdonable", incidía 'Sport 1'.. Gruda parece tener las horas contadas en el Brighton. El RB Leipzig se reservó una opción de compra que entra en vigor en 2027 por una cantidad bastante asequibles: 30 millones de euros. 'Novias', sin embargo, no le faltan. "El Bayern siempre lo ha tenido en su lista, incluso antes de su traspaso al Brighton. No es nada nuevo. Lo han seguido en ventanas de transferencias anteriores también", adelanta Florian Plettenberg. Ha nacido una estrella.

articles.title: 'Now that Walter’s not here…': Scaloni offers Lionel Messi place on Argentina’s coaching staff and backs him to play beyond 2030
articles.summary: Lionel Scaloni opens the door for Lionel Messi's potential return to Argentina's national team in a coaching role after assistant Walter Samuel's departure, emphasizing Messi's continued relevance in football beyond 2030.
articles.body: Lionel Messi may have played his final match for Argentina, but Lionel Scaloni is not ready to let the country's greatest footballer disappear from the national team set-up. With assistant coach Walter Samuel leaving to pursue a new professional challenge, the Argentina manager has found an unexpected replacement candidate. His suggestion came with a smile, but the invitation was genuine: Messi would always be welcome back, even if he returned in a different role.Scaloni jokes about Messi joining Argentina’s coaching staffScaloni raised the possibility of Messi joining his coaching staff after Samuel announced his departure from the Argentina set-up. The former defender, who had been one of Scaloni's assistants during the team's successful run, is leaving to pursue a new professional challenge, creating a vacancy on the coaching staff.Asked about the prospect of Messi returning in a different capacity, Scaloni responded with a playful invitation.“If he wants to come here, there's no problem. Now that Walter's not here...” Scaloni said with a laugh.The remark was light-hearted, but it reflected the manager's desire to keep Messi connected to the national team. The pair worked together through Argentina's transformation into world champions, with Messi central to the team's success at the 2021 Copa América and the 2022 FIFA World Cup.Scaloni also made clear that he hopes Messi continues playing for as long as possible, despite his decision to step away from international football. Speaking ahead of Argentina's friendly against Costa Rica, the coach said he believes the forward could remain active well into the next decade.“I think he will keep playing, and he will carry on even beyond 2030. He has already declined to play for the national team, but I hope, as a footballer, that he continues his career for as long as possible.”Messi's continued excellence at club level offers plenty of reason to believe his playing days are far from over. Still looking remarkably sharp and fit, the Argentine continues to defy expectations at Inter Miami, where he won the 2026 MLS Golden Boot with 26 goals and 17 assists, becoming the first player in league history to claim the honour in consecutive seasons.He also reached 100 goals for the club across all competitions during the 2026 Campeones Cup victory over Cruz Azul and became only the second player in MLS history to score at least 20 goals in three consecutive regular seasons. Such remarkable consistency at this stage of his career underlines that, while his international future may be behind him, Messi still has plenty to offer at club level.Messi’s Argentina career leaves an extraordinary legacyMessi's international journey was not always straightforward. For years, he faced criticism and intense pressure to deliver a major trophy for Argentina, with the disappointment of several near misses leading him to briefly step away from international football in 2016.He eventually returned and changed the course of the national team's history, captaining Argentina to the 2021 Copa América before completing his long-awaited World Cup triumph in Qatar in 2022. The victories helped settle the debate surrounding his place in Argentine football and established him as one of the country's defining sporting figures.Across 208 international appearances, Messi scored 126 goals, making him Argentina's all-time leading scorer. His contribution to the national team extended beyond those numbers, with his leadership and performances central to the success of Scaloni's project.Although his international playing career has come to an end, Messi's relationship with the national team remains strong. Scaloni's comments suggest that the door is open for him to return in a coaching or advisory capacity whenever he is ready.At club level, Messi remains contracted to Inter Miami until December 2028, giving him time to continue his playing career in the United States before considering what comes next.Messi set for return to Buenos Aires as Inter Miami face River PlateMessi is also expected to return to the Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires on January 19, 2027, when Inter Miami face River Plate in a friendly as both clubs prepare for the new season.The fixture will bring him back to one of Argentina's most significant football venues, around three months after his emotional farewell ceremony with the national team. The Monumental has been closely associated with his international career, making the return particularly meaningful for supporters who watched him lead Argentina to its greatest recent achievements.Several prominent players are expected to feature, including Luis Suárez, Nicolás Otamendi and Casemiro. Former La Liga names such as Gonzalo Montiel, Rodrigo De Paul and Ángel Correa are also among those expected to take part.The clubs are yet to announce the full organisational details, ticket-sale arrangements and accompanying events, with further information expected through their official channels.Between Scaloni's invitation to join the coaching staff and his upcoming return to Buenos Aires, Messi's connection with Argentine football is set to continue beyond his final appearance for the national team. The role may eventually change, but his place within the country's football set-up remains open.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
